In [[mathematics]], the '''density topology''' on the [[real number]]s is a [[Topological space|topology]] on the real line that is different (strictly [[Comparison of topologies|finer]]), but in some ways analogous, to the [[Number line#As a topological space|usual topology]].  It is sometimes used in [[real analysis]] to express or relate properties of the [[Lebesgue measure]] in topological terms.

== Definition ==

Let <math>U \subseteq \mathbb{R}</math> be a Lebesgue-measurable set. By the [[Lebesgue density theorem]], almost every point <math>x</math> of <math>U</math> is a density point of <math>U</math>, i.e., satisfies
:<math>\frac{\lambda(U \, \cap \, (x-h,x+h))}{2h} \ \underset{h \to 0^+}{\longrightarrow} \ 1</math>
where <math>\lambda</math> is the Lebesgue measure and <math>(x-h,x+h)</math> is the open interval of length <math>2h</math> centered at <math>x</math>.

When ''all'' points of <math>U</math> are density points of <math>U</math>, it is said to be '''density open'''.<ref>{{harv | Tall | 1976 | loc=definition&nbsp;2.1 }}</ref>

It can be shown that the density open sets of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> form a topology (in other words, they are stable under arbitrary unions and finite intersections):<ref>{{harv | Tall | 1976 | loc=theorem&nbsp;2.3 }}</ref> this constitutes the density topology.

== Examples ==

Every open set in the usual topology of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> (i.e., a union of open intervals) is density open, but the converse is not true. For example, the subset <math>\mathbb{R} \setminus \{1/n : n > 0\}</math> is not open in the usual sense (since every open neighborhood of 0 contains some <math>1/n</math> and is thus not contained in the set), but it ''is'' density open (the only problematic point being 0 and the set has density 1 at 0). More generally, any subset of [[full measure (mathematics)|full measure]] is density open. This includes, for example, the complements of <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> and the [[Cantor set]].

Less trivially, and perhaps more instructively, let us show that the set <math>U := \mathbb{R} \setminus \bigcup_{n=1}^{+\infty} \left[\frac{1}{n}, \frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{2^n}\right]</math> (which, again, is not open in the usual topology) is density open.  Again, at every point <math>x\in U</math> other than 0 this is clear because it is even neighborhood of ''x'' for the usual topology, so the only point to consider is 0.  But if <math>h>0</math> and we let <math>k := \left\lfloor\frac{1}{h}\right\rfloor</math>, then each interval <math>\left[\frac{1}{n}, \frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{2^n}\right]</math> that intersects <math>(-h,h)</math> has <math>n>k</math> so their total measure is <math>\leq 2^{-k}</math>, and <math>\frac{\lambda((-h,+h) \setminus U)}{2h} \leq \frac{2^{-k}}{2h} \leq \frac{2^{-1/h}}{h} \underset{h \to 0^+}{\longrightarrow} 0</math> proving that 0 is indeed a density point of ''U''.

== Properties ==

Let <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> denote the real line endowed with the density topology.

* Like <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with the usual topology, <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> is a [[Hausdorff space|Hausdorff]] (''T<sub>2</sub>'') and [[Tychonoff space|Tychonoff]] (''T<sub>{{frac|3|1|2}}</sub>'') topological space but ''unlike'' the usual topology, it is not [[Normal space|normal]] (''T<sub>4</sub>'').<ref>{{harv | Tall | 1976 | loc=theorem&nbsp;2.4 }}</ref><ref>{{harv | Ciesielski | Larson | Ostaszewski | 1994 | loc=theorem&nbsp;1.2.3(iv) }}</ref>

* A subset <math>Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> is [[Nowhere dense set|nowhere dense]] (for the ''density'' topology) ''iff'' it is [[Meagre set|meagre]] (ditto) ''iff'' it is closed and discrete (ditto) ''iff'' it is a [[null set]] (in the sense of Lebesgue measure).<ref>{{harv | Tall | 1976 | loc=theorem&nbsp;2.7 }}</ref><ref>{{harv | Ciesielski | Larson | Ostaszewski | 1994 | loc=theorem&nbsp;1.2.3(ii) }}</ref>

* The [[Borel set|Borel subsets]] of <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> (for the ''density'' topology) are precisely the Lebesgue-measurable sets;<ref>{{harv | Tall | 1976 | loc=theorem&nbsp;2.6(i) }}</ref> and the [[complete Boolean algebra]] of [[regular open set]]s of <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> can be identified with the "reduced measure algebra", i.e., the Boolean algebra of Lebesgue-measurable sets modulo null sets.

* Like <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with the usual topology, <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> is connected.<ref>{{harv | Tall | 1976 | loc=theorem&nbsp;2.10 }}</ref><ref>{{harv | Ciesielski | Larson | Ostaszewski | 1994 | loc=theorem&nbsp;1.2.3(v) }}</ref>

* Like <math>\mathbb{R}</math> with the usual topology, <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> is a [[Baire space]]; in fact, unlike the usual topology, it is even ''hereditarily Baire'' in the sense that every subspace of <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> is a Baire space.<ref>{{harv | Tall | 1976 | loc=theorem&nbsp;2.11 }}</ref>

* The [[Compact space|compact]] subspaces of <math>\mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}</math> are precisely its finite subsets.<ref>{{harv | Ciesielski | Larson | Ostaszewski | 1994 | loc=theorem&nbsp;1.2.3(vi) }}</ref>

* The [[approximately continuous]] functions <math>f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}</math> are precisely the continuous functions <math>f : \mathbb{R}_{\mathrm{d}}\to\mathbb{R}</math> (i.e., placing the density topology at the source but the usual topology at the target).<ref>{{harv | Ciesielski | Larson | Ostaszewski | 1994 | loc=§1.3 }}</ref>
